4-1.title: Temperature, Thermal Energy, and Heat
4-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Three related ideas:
- Temperature measures how FAST the particles in matter are moving. Faster particles = higher temperature.
- Thermal energy is the TOTAL energy of all the moving particles in an object. (A big object can hold more thermal energy than a small one at the same temperature.)
- Heat is thermal energy that FLOWS from a warmer object to a cooler object.

Key rule: Heat always moves from HOT to COLD until both objects reach the same temperature (this is called reaching thermal equilibrium).

Example 1 — Spoon in soup
Hot soup has fast-moving particles (high temperature). Heat flows from the hot soup to the cooler spoon, so the spoon warms up.

Example 2 — Ice in a drink
Heat flows from the warmer drink INTO the cooler ice, so the drink cools and the ice melts.

Example 3 — Same temperature, different thermal energy
A bathtub of warm water and a cup of warm water can be the same temperature, but the bathtub holds much more thermal energy because it has far more particles.

4-2.title: Heat Transfer: Radiation, Conduction, Convection
4-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Heat moves in three ways:
- Radiation: heat travels as rays (waves) through EMPTY space — no matter needed. This is how the Sun's heat reaches Earth, and how you feel warmth from a fire across a room.
- Conduction: heat passes DIRECTLY between objects that are TOUCHING — like a hot pan warming your hand, or a metal spoon heating up in soup.
- Convection: heat moves in flowing LIQUIDS or GASES. Warm material rises and cool material sinks, making circular convection currents (in air, oceans, boiling water, and Earth's mantle).

Example 1 — Sun's warmth
The Sun warms Earth by RADIATION, because the rays travel through the empty space between them.

Example 2 — Touching a hot stove
Touching a hot pan transfers heat by CONDUCTION because the objects are in direct contact.

Example 3 — Boiling water
In a pot of boiling water, hot water rises and cool water sinks in a loop — that is CONVECTION.

4-3.title: Thermal Energy and Materials
4-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Different materials handle heat differently:
- Conductors let heat flow through them QUICKLY. Most metals (copper, aluminum, iron) are good conductors — that's why a metal spoon in soup gets hot fast.
- Insulators SLOW heat down. Wood, plastic, rubber, cloth, foam, and trapped air are good insulators — that's why oven mitts, jacket fillings, and cup sleeves protect us.

Engineers and inventors choose conductors or insulators ON PURPOSE to control where heat goes.

Example 1 — Pot design
A cooking pot is made of metal (a conductor) so heat moves into the food quickly, but the handle is often plastic or wood (an insulator) so it stays cool to touch.

Example 2 — Staying warm
A winter coat traps air and uses fluffy insulating material to slow body heat from escaping.

Example 3 — Best choice
To keep a drink cold longer, you would choose an INSULATING cup (like foam), not a metal one, because the insulator slows heat from entering.

questions.question: Two spoons sit in hot soup: one metal and one wood. Which gets hot first and why?

choices.B: The metal, because metal is a good conductor

questions.question: Which sentence correctly describes how to keep something cold?

choices.A: Use a conductor to slow heat from entering
choices.B: Use a conductor to speed heat from leaving
choices.C: Use an insulator to slow heat from entering
choices.D: Use any material; it makes no difference

choices.C: Metals are insulators that block heat

questions.question: Which is the BEST material choice for the inside of a foam cooler that keeps food cold?

questions.question: Which statement correctly summarizes conductors and insulators?
